parts.title: Hiring a Community Hall
parts.scenario: A man phones a community centre to hire its hall for his mother's seventieth birthday party.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Janet
voices.desc: Centre bookings manager — female, 50s, brisk but warm, efficient; British accent (southern England)

voices.label: Daniel
voices.desc: Caller — male, 30s, friendly, slightly rushed and disorganised; British accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a community centre to book a room for a family party. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 6.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [telephone rings twice, then the line clicks open] [brisk, friendly] Good morning, Larkfield Community Centre, Janet speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [friendly, slightly rushed] Oh, hello. Um, I'm ringing about hiring one of your rooms for a party. It's for my mum — she's turning seventy, and we wanted to do something a bit special for her.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [warm] Oh, how lovely. Well, you've come to the right place, we do a lot of birthdays. Let me just take a few details first. Could I have your name?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Yes, it's Daniel Cartwell.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [typing, murmuring] Daniel... Cartwright, was that?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [light laugh] Everyone says that. No, it's Cartwell. C... A... R... T... W... E... double L.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [repeating slowly, as if writing it down] C, A, R, T, W, E, double L. Got it, thank you. And what sort of date were you thinking of?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [thinking aloud] Well, her actual birthday is Wednesday the tenth of May, but obviously a weekday's no good for most people, so we were looking at the Saturday after that... the thirteenth.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [apologetic] Ah. [short pause] I'm afraid the thirteenth has gone. We've got a wedding reception in all day. How about the following Saturday?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [hesitant, checking] So that'd be... the twentieth?

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: That's right. The twentieth is completely free at the moment.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [relieved] Then let's go for that. My sister did say she couldn't make the thirteenth anyway, so it's probably for the best.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [efficient] Lovely, I'll pencil you in. And roughly how many guests are you expecting?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [uncertain, a little embarrassed] That's the tricky bit. We sent out sixty invitations, but quite a few people are bringing partners, and Mum keeps adding cousins I've never heard of... [chuckles] so realistically we're planning for about eighty-five.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [thoughtful] Eighty-five. Right, that does narrow things down. Our Willow Room is lovely, but it only takes forty-five, so that's out. The main hall holds two hundred...

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [doubtful] That sounds a bit enormous for us.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [agreeing] It can feel rather empty with a smaller group, yes. So I'd suggest the Orchard Room. It takes up to a hundred, and it opens straight onto the garden, which is nice in May.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [pleased] Oh, that sounds perfect. Mum's a keen gardener.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [informative] Now, the price. On a Saturday the standard rate is forty-five pounds an hour...

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [slightly worried] Ah. Right.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [correcting herself, a little flustered] No, hang on, sorry, that's the main hall. I was looking at the wrong line. The Orchard Room is thirty-eight pounds an hour.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [relieved] Thirty-eight. That's better than I expected. Is there a discount for people who live locally? Someone told me there was.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [regretful] There used to be, but the trustees stopped it last year, I'm afraid.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [good-humoured] Never mind. And what time could we get in? We'd want to put decorations up.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [helpful] The room's free from midday, so you can come in any time after that, but the time you spend decorating does count towards the hire.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [laughs] Then we'll be quick about it. Probably three o'clock until eleven.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [typing] Three till eleven. Now, as for what's included... tables and chairs, of course, and we can lend you white tablecloths at no extra charge. There's a fully equipped kitchen, with plates and cutlery for a hundred.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And glasses?

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [apologetic sigh] We had a set of glasses, but so many got broken that we don't supply them any more. So you'd have to bring your own glasses, or hire some.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [noting it down] Right. I'll ask the caterers, they might have some.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 7 to 10.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [brisk] Now, there are a few other things I should mention. Parking first.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Yes, that'll matter. A lot of Mum's friends drive.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [reassuring] Well, the car park has forty spaces, and it doesn't shut at night, so nobody gets locked in. People used to need a permit to park there, but we got rid of that system a couple of years ago.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Great.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [slightly cautious] The only thing is, there's a yoga class in the studio on Saturday evenings, and they normally take about a dozen of those spaces until half past seven. So your first guests might struggle a little.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [thinking] OK, I'll tell people not to come too early. Now, music. My cousin's band is playing. Is that all right?

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [cheerful] Of course. Our licence runs until midnight on Saturdays. It's only on weekday evenings that things have to stop at eleven.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And would they have to use your sound system?

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: No, they don't need to, most bands prefer their own. [more serious] What we do ask, though, is that you put a short note through the doors of the houses on Mill Lane, at least a week before the party, so they know there'll be some noise. We've had complaints in the past when people weren't warned.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [agreeably] That's fair enough. I can do that.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: And will you be doing the food yourselves?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [laughing] That's been a long family debate. My aunt offered to cook everything, but she's seventy-three herself, and we didn't want her stuck in a kitchen all night. Then someone suggested everybody bringing a dish, but Mum said that would be like asking her guests to pay to come.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [chuckles] I can see her point.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: So in the end we've gone for a local firm, Hollis Catering. They'll bring hot dishes already cooked and just keep them warm in your ovens.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: That's no problem at all. [businesslike] Finally, there's a deposit of a hundred pounds to secure the date, and you get that back as long as the room's left tidy.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Can I pay that now? I've got my card here.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [apologetic] Normally, yes, but our card machine's being replaced this week, so I can't take cards at the moment. And we don't accept bank transfers any more. Our treasurer found it too hard to match payments to bookings.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [slightly puzzled] So...

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: So you'd need to drop it into the office here, cash or a cheque. We're open nine till five on weekdays.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [decisive] I'm driving past on Thursday anyway, so I'll call in then.

script.speaker: Janet
script.text: [warm, wrapping up] Perfect. I'll hold the room until Friday, and once the deposit's in, it's confirmed. And happy birthday to your mum!

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [smiling] Thanks, I'll pass that on. Bye now.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Open Day at Brickfield City Farm
parts.context: Monologue in an everyday social context (volunteer briefing)
parts.scenario: A volunteer coordinator briefs a group of new volunteers before a city farm's open day.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Megan
voices.desc: Volunteer coordinator — female, late 30s, energetic, warm, practical; British accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer coordinator talking to a group of new volunteers about a city farm's open day. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [cheerful, voice slightly raised to address a group] Right, good morning, everyone, and thank you so much for coming along. I'm Megan, I coordinate the volunteers here at Brickfield City Farm, and I'll be your main point of contact on Saturday. I know one or two of you have helped out before, but most of you are new, so I'll go through everything from the beginning.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [warm, explaining] Now, you may have heard that this is our twentieth year, and yes, there will be a cake. [light laugh] A very large one. But the anniversary isn't really why we're holding the open day. Nor is it mainly about money. We'll have collection buckets, of course, but the new roof for the goat barn has already been paid for by a council grant.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [candid, more serious] The honest truth is that we're seriously short of regular helpers, especially on weekday mornings, and an open day is far and away the best way we've found of signing people up. So if anyone shows an interest, please send them to the green gazebo.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [informative] A few things are different from last year. Last time, we charged visitors three pounds at the gate, which caused long queues and, frankly, put some local families off. This year, thanks to a sponsor, there won't be any charge at all. Some people have rung up asking whether they need to book a place online. They don't, they can just turn up. And the hours are exactly the same as before: ten until four.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [lighter, amused] Right, the animals. The rabbits are always the most popular, with the guinea pigs a close second. Children can feed them, we sell little bags of feed for fifty pence, and that's absolutely fine.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [firmer, emphasising] What we don't allow is children walking around holding them. Rabbits wriggle, and if they're dropped they can be badly hurt. So the rule is that the child sits down on the bench first, and then you place the rabbit on a towel on their lap. [casual] Last year we put the rabbits back in their hutches at lunchtime to give them a rest, but in fact they coped perfectly well, so they'll be out all day this time.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [reflective, a little rueful] People often ask me what I worry about most on the day. Parking always looks chaotic from the gate, but it does sort itself out, because the school next door lets us use their playground. And the queue for the café can get long, but people are usually very patient when there's cake involved.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [serious, slowing down] No, what really keeps me awake is the lost children's point. Last year we had eleven children separated from their parents in a single afternoon, and one little boy was missing for nearly forty minutes. So whoever's on that point needs to stay there, and not wander off to help elsewhere.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [practical] And the weather. If it rains, the tractor rides will still run, because the trailer's covered. We used to move the craft tables into the big barn when it rained, but the noise upset the animals, so now they go into the classroom instead. The only activity we'll actually call off is the pony rides. The ground gets far too slippery.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [brisk, orienting the group] OK, if you look at the plan I've given you, I'll show you where everything's going to be on the day. We're standing at the main entrance, at the bottom of the plan, facing into the farm, so north is straight ahead. The main path runs from here up to the duck pond in the middle. It then splits and goes round both sides of the pond, and the two halves join up again on the far side.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [explaining] First aid. In previous years the first-aid post was right beside the café, which is just inside the gate on your left. But it got far too crowded there, so this year it's moving further up on the same side, right against the west fence, just south of the big barn. So it isn't on the main path at all. It's over by the fence.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [emphatic] Now, the lost children's point, and please do remember where this is. Lots of parents assume it'll be at the entrance, and we'll put a sign up here, but the point itself is beyond the pond, at the place where the two paths meet again. So that's on the north side of the pond.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [clear, matter-of-fact] Pony rides. You'd expect them to be in the paddock, but the paddock's being used for the sheep-shearing display this year. So the ponies will be in the small field in the bottom right-hand corner of the site, the south-east corner, to your right as you come in.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [informative] The plant sale is new this year. It'll be along the north fence, at the very top of the plan, halfway between the big barn and the orchard. [slightly apologetic] It won't be inside the orchard itself, I'm afraid, because the trees are being pruned that week.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [wrapping up] And finally, the cheese-making demonstration. Originally we'd planned to have it in the barn, by the door, but there just isn't enough light in there. So it'll be over on the east side of the site, between the orchard and the paddock, right up against the east fence.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [warm, upbeat] Right, that's everything from me. Grab a coffee, and I'll come round and give you your T-shirts.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

question_groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

H = against the west fence, between the Café and the Big Barn, directly south of the barn. I = against the north fence, halfway between the Big Barn and the Orchard.

parts.title: Dissertation: Food-Packaging Waste in Supermarkets
parts.scenario: Two students, Kirsty and Owen, discuss their joint dissertation on food-packaging waste in supermarkets with their tutor, Dr Lawson.
parts.accent: Tutor British (en-GB); Kirsty Australian (en-AU); Owen British (en-GB)

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Dr Lawson
voices.desc: Tutor — male, 50s, calm, measured, dry humour; British accent

voices.label: Kirsty
voices.desc: Student — female, early 20s, lively, direct, enthusiastic; Australian accent

voices.label: Owen
voices.desc: Student — male, early 20s, thoughtful, slightly hesitant; British accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Kirsty and Owen, talking to their tutor about their dissertation on food-packaging waste in supermarkets. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [door closes softly] [welcoming, relaxed] Come in, both of you, have a seat. So, it's been about a month since we last met. How's the packaging project going?

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [upbeat] Pretty well, I think. Though you'll have noticed from the outline that it's changed quite a bit since then.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [curious] Yes, I did. You were originally going to look at plastic waste across the whole retail sector, weren't you? Now it's just food packaging in supermarkets. Was that because of what I said about the scope?

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [slightly sheepish] Well, you did say it was ambitious, and to be fair you were right. But honestly, we'd probably have stuck with it if we could. The real problem was that the council wouldn't give us the waste figures broken down by type of business. They said the data simply wasn't held in that form.

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [agreeing] Whereas the supermarkets publish their own packaging reports, so at least there's something to work with.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [dry] And there I was thinking you'd taken my advice. [chuckles] Still, it's a much tighter project now, and a great deal more manageable. So, you've done your store visits now?

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [enthusiastic] Yeah, three stores, all in the city centre. And some of it wasn't what we expected at all. We'd assumed loose fruit and veg would be dearer than the packaged stuff...

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [interrupting gently] Which it was, in one shop.

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [conceding quickly] In one shop, sure, but in the other two it actually worked out cheaper per kilo. What really struck us was how little room it got. In the biggest store the loose produce took up barely a fifth of the display.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [thoughtful] And the managers kept telling us that loose items get bruised and damaged more, so there's more waste. But honestly, we didn't see much sign of that.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [measured] Interesting. Let's talk about your shopper survey. How many responses have you got?

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [slightly defensive] Sixty-two. We know that's not huge.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [reassuring] For a dissertation, that's perfectly defensible, I wouldn't worry about the numbers. And I know some people would say you should have done it online rather than standing outside shops with clipboards, but face to face tends to get you more thoughtful answers.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [more serious] No, my concern is the wording. Take question four. You ask people whether they agree that supermarkets use far too much unnecessary plastic. You're more or less telling people what to think.

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [wincing, light laugh] Yeah... reading it back, it's not exactly neutral, is it?

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [practical] Then acknowledge that as a limitation, and don't build too much on that question. Now, compostable packaging. You've written quite a lot on that.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [keen] Yes, I think it's one of the more hopeful developments. It does cost the supermarkets more, but...

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [cutting in, firm but friendly] See, the cost isn't really what bothers me. And yes, shoppers get confused about which bin it goes in, but that's true of nearly all packaging. My real problem with it is that our local plant can't actually process it. So it gets sent to landfill with everything else, and nobody's any better off.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [conceding a little] That's true round here. It's not true everywhere, though.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [moving on] Which brings us to the international chapter. Owen, I gather you wanted to add Germany and France?

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [hopeful] I did. The German deposit scheme is fascinating.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [dry] I'm sure it is, but you're already well over the word count. I wouldn't get rid of the chapter altogether, because the comparison does strengthen your argument, but it can't stand on its own.

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [thinking aloud] So... we squeeze it down to a couple of pages and fold it into the literature review?

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: Exactly that.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [resigned, good-humoured sigh] OK. Goodbye, France.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [businesslike] Right, let's go through your main sources, because one or two of them worry me slightly. First, the government report on packaging waste, the one from twenty nineteen.

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [eager] That's our main source for the national figures. We thought we'd check its numbers against the industry ones?

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [gently correcting] You could, but there's no real need. There's an updated edition. It came out last spring, with figures up to twenty twenty-four. You should be using that one rather than the old one.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [surprised] Oh. We had no idea. Right, we'll swap it.

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [slightly dismayed] Though if the figures have changed much, we'll have to redo a couple of our graphs.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [unsympathetic but kind] Probably, yes. But better now than after the examiners have noticed.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: Then the Packaging Industry Alliance website.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [sceptical] Honestly, I'd rather leave that out. They're a lobby group. Of course they say packaging reduces food waste.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [considered] They're not neutral, certainly. But ignoring them completely would look as if you hadn't considered the other side. What I'd do is compare their statistics with the university study from Exeter, and see whether they hold up.

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [agreeing] That makes sense.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: And the television documentary... Wrapped, I think it was called.

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [enthusiastic] Oh, I love that one. I was going to quote the presenter in our introduction. She's got this brilliant line about plastic mountains.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [amused, but firm] It's a good line, but a documentary isn't evidence in academic terms. It's fine for giving you a feel for the debate, but I wouldn't cite it.

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [slightly disappointed] OK, so it's just something we watched to get our heads round the issue, then.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: The PhD thesis from Leeds, by Dr Okafor?

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [keen] Yeah, that one's really close to what we're doing. Kirsty thought we could borrow her questionnaire design...

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [light laugh] But our survey's already done, so that's a bit late now.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [thoughtful] Quite. But she mentions that she collected weekly store data she didn't have space to analyse. If I were you, I'd email her and ask whether she'd share it. Researchers are usually happy to.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [pleased] That would save us weeks.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: And lastly, the newspaper interview with the chief executive of Fairway supermarkets.

script.speaker: Kirsty
script.text: [uncertain] We weren't sure about that one. Newspapers aren't exactly peer-reviewed.

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: Normally I'd agree. But it's the only time anyone at that level has admitted publicly that their targets won't be met, so his exact words matter. Use them, word for word, in quotation marks.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [hesitant] Should we put the whole article in an appendix as well?

script.speaker: Dr Lawson
script.text: [mild, unhurried] No, I wouldn't bother with that. The quotation's enough. Right, shall we look at your timetable?

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: The History and Science of Glassmaking
parts.scenario: A lecturer gives a talk on what glass is and how glassmaking developed from the ancient world to the present.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Lecturer
voices.desc: University lecturer — female, 40s, articulate, lively, occasionally wry; British accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the history and science of glassmaking. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture theatre, faint murmur fading] [lively, clear] Good afternoon, everyone. Today we're turning to a material that's so familiar we hardly notice it: glass. I want to look first at what glass actually is, and then trace how people learned to make it, and to make it better, over roughly four and a half thousand years.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining carefully] So, the science. Most of the solids we think of as hard, metals, salt, ice, are crystalline. Their atoms are lined up in a neat, repeating lattice, rather like soldiers on parade. Glass isn't like that. When you examine its structure, the arrangement of the atoms is random. It's essentially the structure of a liquid that's been frozen in place before it had time to organise itself.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [wry] This has given rise to a famous myth, which I'm sure some of you have heard: that glass is really a very slow-moving liquid, and that's why old church windows are thicker at the bottom. It isn't true. Calculations suggest that glass at room temperature wouldn't flow noticeably in the entire lifetime of the universe. The thick bottoms are simply because glaziers tended to put the heavier edge of an uneven pane at the bottom.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] The main ingredient of most glass is silica, which in practice means sand. The difficulty is that pure silica only melts at around seventeen hundred degrees Celsius, far hotter than any ancient furnace could reach. So glassmakers added soda, that is, sodium carbonate, which brings the melting point down dramatically. An ingredient that does this job is known as a flux, and do note that word, because you'll meet it again and again in the literature.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] But soda on its own creates a problem. Soda glass is chemically unstable. Strange as it sounds, it will slowly dissolve in water. People often guess that it's acid that attacks it, but in fact ordinary rain is quite enough, given time. The solution was to add lime, which acts as a stabiliser, and that combination of sand, soda and lime is still the basis of about ninety per cent of the glass made today.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [shifting tone, narrative] Now to the history. The oldest glass objects we know of come from Mesopotamia, from about four and a half thousand years ago. You might imagine cups or bottles, but those didn't appear for another thousand years or so. The earliest objects were beads: small, brightly coloured, and treated almost like precious stones.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [enthusiastic] The real revolution came in the first century BC, probably somewhere along the coast of what's now Syria, with the invention of glassblowing. Instead of slowly shaping glass around a core, a worker could gather molten glass on the end of a hollow tube and blow it into shape in a matter of seconds. Suddenly, glass was cheap.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] The Romans adopted the technique with great enthusiasm. They did make some window glass, though it was thick and not very transparent. But the commonest use for blown glass was containers. Now, you might expect these held wine. In fact wine was mostly kept in clay jars called amphorae, which were cheaper and far less fragile. Glass was particularly valued for perfume, because unlike clay, it doesn't absorb the scent or alter it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [narrative] Let's jump forward to medieval Venice, which became the centre of European glassmaking. In twelve ninety-one the city ordered all its glassmakers to move to the nearby island of Murano. You'll often read that this was done to protect trade secrets, and it certainly helped with that. But the official reason given in the decree was the danger of fire. Venice was a crowded city full of wooden buildings, and the furnaces burned day and night.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining] Murano's great achievement was a glass called cristallo, which was almost colourless. Ordinary glass had a greenish tint, which comes from iron in the sand. It isn't caused by copper, as is sometimes claimed; copper tends to give a blue colour. The Venetians found that adding a small amount of manganese cancelled out the green, which is why manganese is sometimes nicknamed glassmaker's soap.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] In England, in the sixteen seventies, George Ravenscroft began adding lead oxide to his glass. People assume lead glass must be stronger, but it's actually rather softer, which makes it easier to cut. What it gained was brilliance. Lead makes glass bend light much more, so when it's cut into facets, it sparkles. [dry] That's the origin of what we call lead crystal, which, ironically, given what I said earlier, isn't a crystal at all.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [moving on] For centuries, making flat glass for windows remained difficult. You either blew a large cylinder and cut it open, or spun a disc. Both methods left the glass slightly wavy and uneven. The breakthrough came in the nineteen fifties with the float process, developed by Alastair Pilkington in Britain.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining clearly] In the float process, molten glass is poured continuously onto a bath of molten tin. People sometimes assume mercury was used, because it's liquid at room temperature, but it boils far too easily. Tin stays liquid over the whole working range, and because its surface is perfectly flat, the glass floating on top ends up perfectly flat as well. Almost all window glass is made this way today.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Finally, a word about safety glass. Toughened glass is made by heating ordinary glass and then cooling the outside very quickly using jets of air. Water was tried, but it cools the surface so violently that the glass simply cracks. This rapid cooling puts the surface under compression, which makes the glass several times stronger. And if it does break, it shatters into small, blunt pieces rather than dangerous shards.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [wrapping up, friendly] Next week we'll look at more modern uses, glass in fibre-optic cables and so on, so please read chapter six before then.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.

items.trap: Copper is mentioned as a mistaken explanation.

items.evidence: What it gained was brilliance.

items.evidence: molten glass is poured continuously onto a bath of molten tin
